before.title: Automatic Transmission Torque-Converter Lockup Shudder and Slipping
before.description: The Aisin-based 4-speed automatic (V4AW2/V4AW3) behind the Montero V6 develops a torque-converter lockup (damper-clutch) shudder as it ages, felt as a vibration or 'buzz' typically in the 35-50 mph range at steady throttle that owners often mistake for an engine misfire. A Mitsubishi TSB attributes this to breakdown of the ATF causing damper-clutch shudder (documented for 1999-2003 Montero/Montero Sport; on RWD trucks it can also cause rear leaf-spring chatter). Neglected or overheated fluid, common on trucks that tow or wheel, also leads to worn clutch packs, slipping, delayed engagement, and harsh or missed shifts.
before.solution: Start with the fluid: use the correct ATF, correct level, and inspect condition; a fluid service (and a friction-modifier additive in mild cases) frequently reduces or eliminates lockup shudder. Verify the throttle position sensor and transmission temperature/pressure inputs. Add or service an auxiliary transmission cooler on trucks used for towing/off-road. Persistent slipping or clutch-pack wear requires a transmission rebuild and torque-converter replacement.
symptoms: Shudder or vibration around 35-50 mph (lockup engagement)
Slipping or flaring between gears
Delayed or harsh engagement into Drive/Reverse
Stuck in a single gear (limp mode)
Burnt-smelling or dark ATF

before.title: Crankshaft Position Sensor / Distributor Pickup Failure (Crank-No-Start and Stalling)
before.description: The 6G72's crank/cam timing signal on early 1990s trucks is generated inside the distributor, and later trucks use a discrete crankshaft position sensor at the front of the engine behind the crank pulley/timing covers. As these sensors and their pickups age they fail intermittently, producing a classic 'cranks but won't start' condition or sudden stalling while driving that often clears after the engine cools. Owners repeatedly report that aftermarket sensors do not resolve the problem and that only a genuine Mitsubishi (OEM) sensor restores reliable operation; the crank sprocket tone/reluctor ring can also strip or be damaged.
before.solution: Test the crank sensor/ignition pickup output per the factory procedure before replacing parts. Replace the failed crankshaft position sensor (or the distributor pickup on early trucks) with a genuine OEM Mitsubishi unit, as aftermarket units are widely reported to be unreliable here. Inspect the crank sprocket/tone ring for stripping or damage. Address related ignition coil/power transistor faults that can mimic the same stall.
symptoms: Engine cranks but will not start
Sudden stall while driving, restarts after cooling
Intermittent no-spark condition
Hard starting when hot
Check engine light for crank sensor circuit (OBD-II trucks)

before.title: Super Select 4WD Vacuum Actuator / Free-Wheel Engagement Failure
before.description: The Montero's Super Select 4WD (second-generation, 1992+) engages the front axle through a vacuum-operated free-wheel actuator and electric solenoids rather than a mechanical linkage from the shifter. Over decades the dual-solenoid pack fails, the rubber hoses deteriorate, and the front differential actuator (a small shaft under a rubber boot on the passenger side of the front diff) can rust or seize, especially after long storage. The result is a truck that will not engage or disengage 4WD properly, gets stuck in 2WD or 4WD, grinds from the front axle, or flashes the 4WD indicator lights. This is a signature, well-documented failure mode discussed extensively in the overland/Expedition Portal community.
before.solution: Diagnose with a hand vacuum pump: apply vacuum to the free-wheel actuator, confirm it strokes fully into 4WD and holds vacuum. Replace failed 4WD select solenoid valves, cracked vacuum hoses, and a rusted vacuum reservoir; free or replace a seized front-axle actuator. Verify the front-axle detection switch and transfer-case position switches, and clean/reseal connectors. On later/OBD-II trucks, read the transfer-case control codes to isolate the failed component.
symptoms: 4WD will not engage or will not release
Front-wheel/4WD indicator lights flashing
Stuck in 2WD or stuck in 4WD
Grinding noise from the front axle on engagement
Difficulty shifting the transfer case between ranges

before.title: Timing Belt Failure on Interference Engine (6G72/6G74) Causes Bent Valves
before.description: Both the 3.0L 6G72 and the 3.5L 6G74 V6s used in the 1990s Montero are interference-design engines driven by a rubber timing belt. If the belt snaps, or if it is contaminated by oil leaking from the front cover/cam seals, the pistons strike the open valves and bend them. Note that while the generic 12-valve SOHC 3.0L in some Chrysler/Dodge applications is often called non-interference, the 6G72 as installed in the Mitsubishi Montero/Diamante is confirmed by engine references and owners to be an interference motor, and the 6G74 is interference as well. Many 90s Monteros are now well past any documented belt service, making this the single most consequential neglected item on the platform.
before.solution: Replace the timing belt on the factory interval (roughly every 60,000 miles / ~7 years), and replace the tensioner, idler, and water pump at the same time since they share the same access. Fix any front cover or cam/crank seal leaks that could oil-soak the belt. If a belt has already broken, install a new belt/tensioner set and perform a compression or borescope check for bent valves before returning the engine to service; bent valves require head removal and valve replacement.
symptoms: Engine cranks but will not start after belt snaps
Sudden loss of power while driving
Rattling or slapping noise from front timing cover before failure
Rough running or dead cylinders after a belt event
Low or zero compression on affected cylinders

before.title: Valve Stem Seal Wear and High Oil Consumption on High-Mileage V6s
before.description: As the 6G72 and 6G74 V6s age, the valve stem seals harden and crack and the piston rings/valve guides wear, allowing oil into the combustion chamber. This is one of the most widely reported 90s Montero engine complaints. Owners report consumption on the order of a quart every 1,000-1,500 miles with bluish smoke that is worst on cold startup (after the engine sits, oil seeps past the seals and burns off in a plume) and on deceleration. Note that the underlying cause is often worn valve guides, so seal replacement can be a band-aid; Mitsubishi's own spec treats ~1 quart/1,000 miles as within range for this engine family.
before.solution: Replace the valve stem seals (often done with the heads on using a spring compressor and air-hold tool, otherwise heads are removed) and inspect the valve guides, since worn guides are the frequent root cause. Confirm the source with a leak-down test to distinguish seals/guides (smoke mainly on startup/decel) from worn rings (smoke under load/all the time). Verify PCV system operation; if rings are the cause, plan for a more involved rebuild.
symptoms: Blue/gray smoke from exhaust on cold startup
Puff of smoke on deceleration or after idling
Elevated oil consumption (roughly a quart every 1,000-1,500 miles)
Fouled spark plugs
Oily deposits at tailpipe

proposal.title: Valve Stem Seal Wear and High Oil Consumption on High-Mileage V6s
proposal.description: The reviewed exact manufacturer-communication and recall corpora contain no record establishing recurring valve-stem-seal hardening, worn valve guides, piston-ring wear, a quart-per-1,000-to-1,500-mile pattern or one 1990-1999 Montero V6 population. Smoke timing and oil consumption can help structure diagnosis but do not by themselves distinguish external leakage, PCV ingestion, valve seals and guides, cylinder wear or piston rings. The statement that Mitsubishi treats approximately one quart per 1,000 miles as normal is not supported by an exact primary source in this audit.
proposal.solution: Measure oil consumption over a controlled interval with the oil filled and checked consistently, and inspect external leaks and the PCV and intake paths first. Document plug deposits, smoke conditions, compression, leak-down and borescope findings, then measure valve-guide clearance or cylinder and ring condition as the applicable service procedure requires. Do not buy valve-stem seals, guides, a PCV valve, piston rings, cylinder heads or an engine rebuild kit from this page; the exact oil path, wear measurement and engine fitment must be proven first.
